title: Ser, estar and how you feel
objectives: I can ask and answer Como você está? and say how I feel.
I can describe people with adjectives that agree in gender and number.
I can choose between ser and estar in simple sentences.
I can say what my job is and ask what other people do.
I can make negative sentences with não and ask questions with quem, como, onde and o que.

dialogues.title: How are you today?
dialogues.context: Ana and Carlos meet in the street after work. Ana has had a long day at the hospital.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Oi, Carlos! Como você está?
lines.en: Hi, Carlos! How are you?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Oi, Ana! Estou bem, obrigado. E você?
lines.en: Hi, Ana! I am fine, thank you. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Estou muito cansada. Estou com sono.
lines.en: I am very tired. I am sleepy.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Você está ocupada hoje?
lines.en: Are you busy today?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Estou, sim. Sou enfermeira e estou no hospital hoje.
lines.en: Yes, I am. I am a nurse and I am at the hospital today.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Enfermeira? Que legal! Eu sou professor.
lines.en: A nurse? How cool! I am a teacher.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Professor? Você não é engenheiro?
lines.en: A teacher? Aren't you an engineer?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Não, eu não sou engenheiro. Sou professor.
lines.en: No, I am not an engineer. I am a teacher.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Desculpa, Carlos! Hoje estou muito cansada.
lines.en: Sorry, Carlos! Today I am very tired.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Tudo bem, Ana. Até logo!
lines.en: That's fine, Ana. See you later!

dialogues.title: Who is that?
dialogues.context: Pedro and Marina are at a party. Pedro asks Marina about two people he does not know.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Marina, quem é ele?
lines.en: Marina, who is he?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Ele é o Rafael. Ele é meu amigo.
lines.en: He is Rafael. He is my friend.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Ele é engenheiro?
lines.en: Is he an engineer?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: É, sim. E é muito simpático e engraçado.
lines.en: Yes, he is. And he is very nice and funny.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: E ela? Quem é ela?
lines.en: And her? Who is she?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Ela é a Paula. Ela é médica.
lines.en: She is Paula. She is a doctor.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Ela é muito bonita! E alta.
lines.en: She is very pretty! And tall.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: É, e é muito inteligente também.
lines.en: Yes, and she is very intelligent too.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Onde ela está?
lines.en: Where is she?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Ela está aqui, com o Rafael.
lines.en: She is here, with Rafael.

dialogues.title: A phone call to a sick friend
dialogues.context: Camila calls her friend Bruno, who did not go to work today.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Alô, Bruno! Onde você está?
lines.en: Hello, Bruno! Where are you?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Oi, Camila! Estou em casa. Hoje eu estou doente.
lines.en: Hi, Camila! I am at home. Today I am sick.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Que pena! Como você está?
lines.en: What a pity! How are you?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Estou mal, mas não estou triste.
lines.en: I am unwell, but I am not sad.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Você está com fome?
lines.en: Are you hungry?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Estou, sim! E também estou com sede.
lines.en: Yes, I am! And I am also thirsty.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Eu não sou médica, mas sou amiga.
lines.en: I am not a doctor, but I am a friend.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Você é muito simpática, Camila. Obrigado!
lines.en: You are very nice, Camila. Thank you!

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: De nada! Tchau, Bruno.
lines.en: You're welcome! Bye, Bruno.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Tchau!
lines.en: Bye!

grammar.title: Ser and estar in the present
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese has two verbs for to be: ser and estar. You already know ser from unit 1. Estar is also irregular and must be learned as a block. The stress falls on the last syllable of eu estou (es-TOH), você está (es-TAH) and vocês estão (es-TOWN, with a nasal ending).

As with ser, you only need to learn four forms of estar: estou, está, estamos and estão. Você, ele, ela and a gente all use the same form, and vocês, eles and elas all use the same form. Nós estamos is correct, but in everyday speech a gente takes está.

In fast, informal speech Brazilians shorten estar by dropping the first syllable: estou becomes tô, está becomes tá and estão becomes tão. You will hear Tô cansado and Tá bem all the time. Use the full forms when you write or speak carefully, and understand the short ones when you listen. The verb ser is not normally shortened in this way.

grammar.title: Choosing between ser and estar
grammar.explanation:
English uses one verb, to be, where Portuguese uses two. A useful starting rule is that ser tells you what someone or something is, and estar tells you where they are or how they are right now.

Use ser for identity (Eu sou o Paulo), origin and nationality (Ela é do Brasil), profession (Ele é médico), and lasting characteristics such as height, personality and looks (Ela é alta, ele é simpático). With professions you usually drop the article: Sou professor, not Sou um professor.

Use estar for location (Estou em casa, Ela está no hospital) and for conditions that change: feelings, health, moods and how you are at the moment (Estou cansado, Ele está triste, Nós estamos com fome). The question Como você está? asks how you are feeling now. Feelings like hunger, thirst and sleepiness use estar com followed by the noun: estar com fome, com sede, com sono.

Many adjectives can go with either verb, and the choice changes the meaning. Ele é feliz means he is a happy person in general. Ele está feliz means he is happy at this moment. Ela é bonita says she is pretty, and Ela está bonita says she looks pretty today. The preposition no is em + o and na is em + a, so no hospital means at the hospital and na escola means at school. There is no article in em casa.

grammar.title: Adjective agreement and professions
grammar.explanation:
Adjectives in Portuguese agree with the noun or pronoun they describe, in gender and in number. This applies after both ser and estar. A woman says Estou cansada and a man says Estou cansado. A group of women says Estamos cansadas, and a mixed group or a group of men says Estamos cansados.

Most adjectives ending in -o change to -a for the feminine: alto, alta; bonito, bonita. Adjectives ending in -e, such as inteligente and triste, and those ending in -z or -l, such as feliz, keep the same form for both genders. For the plural, add -s to a vowel: altos, altas, inteligentes. Adjectives ending in -z add -es: felizes. The written accent stays in simpático, simpática, simpáticos, simpáticas.

Professions follow the same pattern. Many end in -o and change: médico, médica; engenheiro, engenheira; advogado, advogada; enfermeiro, enfermeira. Nouns ending in -or add -a: professor, professora. Nouns ending in -ista or -ante keep the same form for both genders and use the article to show gender: o motorista, a motorista; o estudante, a estudante.

When the pronoun is a gente, the adjective still agrees with the real people: a gente está cansado if the group is men, or a gente está cansada if it is women. Muito before an adjective means very and does not change: muito cansada, muito simpáticos.

examples.pt: Ele é alto e ela é alta.
examples.en: He is tall and she is tall.

examples.pt: Ela é professora e ele é professor.
examples.en: She is a teacher and he is a teacher.

grammar.title: Negation and question words
grammar.explanation:
To make a sentence negative, put não directly before the verb: Eu não sou médico, Ela não está em casa. The order of the other words does not change. In short answers you can say the word twice, as in Não, não sou, where the first não answers the question and the second negates the verb. You can also just say Não.

To answer yes, repeat the verb: Você é brasileiro? Sou. or Você está cansada? Estou, sim. Portuguese prefers this to a bare sim.

Yes and no questions have the same word order as statements, with rising intonation at the end: Você é professor? Information questions start with a question word. Quem asks who, como asks how, onde asks where and o que asks what. The verb usually follows: Quem é ele? Onde você está? O que é isso? In spoken Portuguese the question word sometimes comes at the end instead, as in Você está onde?

Compare Como ele é? and Como ele está? The first uses ser and asks what he is like, which is a question about character and looks. The second uses estar and asks how he is at the moment, which is a question about feelings or health. Isso is a neutral word for that or this, as in O que é isso?

culture.title: Talking about how you feel in Brazil
culture.text:
When a Brazilian asks Tudo bem? or Como você está?, the expected answer is usually short and positive: Tudo bem, Estou bem or just Tudo. But it is also normal to be honest about being tired, hungry or busy. People often say Tô cansado or Tô morrendo de fome, and another common answer is mais ou menos, which means so-so. Brazilian conversation is warm, and sharing how you feel is a way to connect.

One word you will hear often is saudade. It describes missing someone or something, and there is no exact English translation. Estou com saudade de você means I miss you. Like fome and sede, it uses estar com.

For professions, Brazilians often ask O que você faz? to find out someone's job, and you answer with ser: Sou professor or Sou engenheira. Titles are important in some settings. Doutor and doutora are used for doctors and lawyers, and often for anyone in a professional role, even if the person does not have a doctorate. Professor and professora are also used as titles when speaking to a teacher directly, as in Bom dia, professora!

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I am tired' (said by a man)?
exercises.explanation: Tiredness is a temporary state, so use estar, and a man uses the masculine cansado.
Profession uses ser, and ela takes é.

exercises.prompt: Where is Pedro? Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: Location uses estar, and ele or a single name takes está.

exercises.prompt: A Ana é ___. Which adjective agrees with Ana and means nice?
exercises.explanation: Ana is one woman, so you need the feminine singular form.
Adjectives ending in -z add -es in the plural.

choices: He is a happy person in general.

exercises.explanation: Não goes directly before the verb.
Profession uses ser, and eles takes são.
The adjective agrees with eles, so it is plural.
Use estar for a temporary state.
Não goes before the verb and médica is feminine.
Hunger is expressed with estar com fome.
